summary: Micah 2 begins with people who plan wrongdoing at night and carry it out by taking fields, houses, and family inheritances. Yahweh answers their planning with an announced disaster, while the people resist unwelcome prophecy and prefer reassuring lies. The chapter closes with a promise that Jacob and the remnant of Israel will be gathered like a flock, with Yahweh at their head.
whyItMatters: This chapter states one of Micah’s central accusations: powerful people are using their power to dispossess others while rejecting words of warning. It also shows Micah’s pattern of placing restoration hope beside judgment, without erasing the charge that caused the judgment.

context.author: The book’s heading attributes the word to Micah of Moresheth; later arrangement of the book is not identified.
context.audience: The speeches address Jacob, Israel, Judah’s communities, and especially people with power over land, households, and public religious speech.
context.date: Micah’s named prophetic setting belongs to the eighth century BCE under Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah of Judah; the date of the finished book is not supplied and is debated.
context.setting: Israel and Judah, with attention to towns, houses, fields, inheritance, assemblies, prophets, and the pressure of coming judgment and restoration.
context.literaryForm: Prophetic accusation, disputed speech, lament, judgment announcement, and restoration promise.

outline.heading: Planned injustice
outline.note: Those with power devise evil and then seize fields, houses, and inheritances from others.

outline.heading: A disaster planned against the planners
outline.note: Yahweh announces that the people who divided others’ possessions will face loss, lament, and exclusion from land allotment in Yahweh’s assembly.

outline.heading: Rejected prophecy
outline.note: Some resist prophecy about disgrace, while the reply asks whether Yahweh’s words do good to the blameless.

outline.heading: The people as an enemy
outline.note: The accusation names stripped travelers, displaced women, and children deprived of blessing, then commands departure from a polluted resting place.

outline.heading: Preferred falsehood
outline.note: A lying prophet who promises wine and strong drink would fit what this people wants to hear.

outline.heading: Gathered like a flock
outline.note: The chapter ends with Yahweh gathering Jacob and the remnant of Israel, with a leader breaking the way open and Yahweh at their head.

keyVerses.text: Woe to those who devise iniquity and work evil on their beds! When the morning is light, they practice it, because it is in the power of their hand.
keyVerses.why: This opening charge shows that the wrongdoing is deliberate and enabled by power.

keyVerses.text: They covet fields and seize them, and houses, then take them away. They oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage.
keyVerses.why: The chapter’s social wrong is concrete: land, homes, households, and inheritance are being taken.

keyVerses.text: If a man walking in a spirit of falsehood lies, saying, “I will prophesy to you of wine and of strong drink,” he would be the prophet of this people.
keyVerses.why: This verse names the problem of welcomed false reassurance in contrast to Micah’s warning.

keyVerses.text: I will surely assemble all of you, Jacob. I will surely gather the remnant of Israel. I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as a flock in the middle of their pasture. They will swarm with people.
keyVerses.why: The judgment speech turns to gathering, making restoration part of the chapter’s final movement.

themes: departure from a ruined resting place

questions.question: What wrong does the chapter accuse people of doing?
questions.answer: The chapter accuses them of planning evil and then using available power to carry it out. The wrong is not left vague: they covet and seize fields and houses, oppressing a man, his household, and his heritage.

questions.question: Why is the night-and-morning sequence important?
questions.answer: Verse 1 pictures people devising iniquity on their beds and practicing it when morning comes. The point is deliberate planning followed by action, not a sudden mistake or impulse.

questions.question: What does “heritage” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: In verse 2, “heritage” is tied to a man, his house, fields, and houses. In this setting it refers to inherited family possession or standing, so the seizure is more than a simple purchase or transfer.

questions.question: How does Yahweh answer the people’s planning?
questions.answer: The people devise iniquity, and Yahweh says he is planning disaster against them. The chapter presents this as a reversal: those who used power to take from others will face a time when they cannot walk haughtily or control the outcome.

questions.question: What is happening in the lament about divided land?
questions.answer: Verse 4 imagines a future lament in which the people say they are ruined and their possession has been divided up. This answers the earlier seizure of fields and houses: loss of land becomes part of the announced judgment.

questions.question: Why do some say, “Don’t prophesy”?
questions.answer: Verse 6 shows resistance to prophecy that announces disgrace. The chapter does not give a full psychological explanation, but verse 11 suggests that a message of wine and strong drink would be more welcome than Micah’s accusation and warning.

questions.question: Does “uncleanness” here mean moral guilt or ritual impurity?
questions.answer: The chapter connects uncleanness with destruction and the loss of a resting place. Against its accusations of robbery and displacement, the place is depicted as polluted and unfit for rest. No ritual procedure is described, and the word should not be separated from the wrongdoing charged in the surrounding verses.

questions.question: Who is the “remnant of Israel”?
questions.answer: Verse 12 uses the phrase for the people Yahweh promises to gather. The chapter does not define their full identity or timeline; it pictures them as Jacob and Israel assembled like sheep in a pasture.

questions.question: Who is the one who breaks open the way?
questions.answer: Verse 13 pictures a way opened through a gate: the people break through, their king passes before them, and Yahweh is at their head. It does not name the king or explain whether the breaker and king are distinct figures. Its focus is on the gathered people being led out under royal and divine leadership.

glossary.def: Wrongdoing named in verse 1 as something deliberately devised before it is practiced.
The family possession or inheritance being taken when fields and houses are seized.
In verse 4, a saying or taunt taken up against the judged people as they lament their loss.
The gathered survivors or remaining people of Israel whom Yahweh promises to assemble.
A place name used in the flock image: the gathered people are compared to the sheep of Bozrah.
